title: Region controls preserve different wiring and cell-mix links in 171 IBL mouse regions
abstract: We tested whether additive region identity and mean division-pair differences explain the reported wiring-versus-cell-mix split in 171 IBL mouse regions. We rebuilt the Knox, Allen CCF and MERFISH predictors and reproduced the prior pair model. We then added an effect for each region and an intercept for each unordered division pair. In this strict model, input wiring predicted task-coding similarity (beta 0.2104; region-jackknife 95 percent interval 0.0736 to 0.3472), while cell mix predicted intrinsic spike similarity (0.1941; 0.0678 to 0.3204). Spatial surrogate tests with 999 draws per family gave Holm-adjusted p = 0.002 for both planned coefficients. Wiring share was 0.988 for coding and 0.144 for intrinsic spiking; the difference was 0.844 with jackknife interval 0.379 to 1.309. But input wiring added only 0.584 percentage points of coding variance, and cell mix added 0.448 percentage points of intrinsic variance. The latter was 79.6 percent smaller than in the prior model. The split kept its sign after each division deletion. The intrinsic input link was unresolved under the spatial null (descriptive p = 0.060). These are small conditional associations in reused region averages, not a causal split or an independent animal replication. Spatial null assumptions and atlas errors remain. Code, all deletion and null fits, a projection derivation, input hashes and external retrieval steps are supplied; Allen-derived regional tables are excluded.

display.caption: Structural coefficients under the prior model, region effects and division-pair controls. Bars show strict-model unique variance. Error bars are region-jackknife 95 percent intervals. They do not account for all spatial dependence.
